title: Legal use of a script you paid for.

posts.author: Arcaines
posts.body:
Hello everyone o/ so a lot of the time I wonder about things and this one came to mind.
If I paid a person to code me a battle system to use in my RPG maker game and I paid him, say £2,000 because it's a complex battle system I wanted.
Can he, afterwards make the code public for people to use? Or can I say, "this is a private script, I don't want it made public"
now, do I have some legal ownership of the script? Or since I've only paid for it the coder can do what he wants with it afterwards?
What are your thoughts?
Personnel myself I can't see any coder doing this as it just wouldn't be professional of them at all.

posts.author: ZimXero
posts.body: It's all in the contract you agree on together.  Nearly anything can be made binding by contract, as long as it does not violate other laws.

posts.author: Andar
posts.body:
Ideally, those question should be handled before the payment is decided.
necause they can affect said payment, a non-exclusive commission can for example be cheaper than an exclusive one.
If no one mentions anything before the commission is completed, it is usually considered an exclusive one (which means no one but the commissioner can use the result).
For example many artists post as part of their commission rules "I can publish the result in my portfolio but not use it elsewhere, a private commission costs +x%"
Or some artist post "the commissioner can use this picture for non-commercial uses, in case of commercial use additional fees apply"
Since those were posted as part of the commission rules, they would apply.
so it depends on what was posted and said by either one of you before the commission was agreed upon.

posts.author: Ms Littlefish
posts.body: Yeah. This is all in the contract/agreement. If you’re buying something that major…make sure there is one. Exclusivity for use is pretty common for private commissions, but buying out their complete right and ownership is another. And, that’d typically cost a fair amount more than just exclusive use of the asset. They can make the code public later if the contract allows so, and quite a few people will cut a deal if you let them share/sell elsewhere.

posts.author: Trihan
posts.body: I'll generally agree this with the client before I start work. Or they'll tell me when they make the request what terms of distribution they want. Either way, I'll always go with what the client wants; if they don't want it public, I won't post it. If they give the go-ahead for it, I will. Sometimes they'll ask for exclusivity for a set period and then it becomes public domain.

posts.author: ATT_Turan
posts.body:
That's a huge amount of money for a plugin, even for something as significant as a battle system.
If I were considering spending (or charging) even hundreds of dollars for a single item, I'd want a full, properly-written contract. I can't imagine paying someone thousands of dollars with no paperwork, just on good will.
(I also can't imagine what you'd want done, outside of maybe turning RPG Maker into some kind of 3D fighting game engine or something, that would cost that much...but that's not the point of the question)

technically no, because it's a product made "to order".
you would be the intellectual artist, since you called the shots and he just wrote it.
that's the whole point and definition of "intellectual property".
people got badly accustomed to pairing "idea" with "product".
just as you'd be obligated to put him in the credits as *coder* of such product, he can't take that idea from you, for his use.

I think it was confusing to people that you apparently have no actual experience with commissioning anything, but you introduced what seemed like a pretty specific example.
Your question would've stood on its own if you simply asked "what is standard, or can I ask for this" without trying to tie it to a theoretical huge amount of money on a single asset
